I guess the "easiest" way would be to argue for the original definition of marriage. Like you said, its a man purchasing a woman. Kinda like how Sherbert isn't really considered ice-cream, but it's own kind of frozen treat.

Marriage carries religious, legal, and cultural elements. It's the religious element that most people have a problem with. While laws and culture evolve, religions do not since those people still refer to texts written thousands of years ago by God knows whom. I actually can understand why a priest should be allowed to refuse to marry a gay couple. You are basically asking him to violate his religious beliefs because of today's political movements.
Look at Christianity as major league baseball. MLB has its own set of rules. Now, a new team wants to join the league. But they say every batter has 4 strikes instead of 3. You try to explain to them that if MLB implements their rule, it's no longer MLB because that's how the rules were laid out. We are not talking about a minor rule change but something that fundamentally changes the game. I'm not taking sides, but I can certainly understand it from the preacher's point of view. You can't ask him to accept something which goes against his own beliefs. However, he should never perform a marriage for a couple where one or both have divorced. You can't treat gays as pariahs and not divorcees because that would be hypocritical.

I had a college professor who did this rather well. He was a very republican man, but the difference is he was more than willing to have constructive discussions (not arguments) about his and other people's beliefs. His belief was that marriage as a concept was deeply tied in his religion (Christianity), and that as a result the government shouldn't be able to dictate whether or not he should be forced to accept gay marriage. That being said, he also recognized that gay couples had the right to get the same legal benefits that a marriage between a heterosexual couple would have. So, in his opinion, he thought it should be a legal partnership, not a marriage.

I'm not saying I agree with his views, but it's food for thought that it's possible to be against "gay marriage" without also being completely against gay people having the same benefits as any other legal partnership.

Abrahamic religions tend to have a very strict definition of marriage, based on their versions of morality. Recently that has been "streamlined" to include only one man and woman woman.

If we're saying that that should have no influence on today's civil institution of marriage, then a lot of our restrictions on marriage similarly don't make any sense.

Polygamy: An arguement for convenience could be made here (how do you divide property between multiple spouses) But what if someone wants to marry one man and one woman? What purpose does the civil government have interfering here?

Incest: Between two consenting adults, the only issues are moral ones, and why should the state impose here? An arguement could be made that such a couple has an increased risk of birth defects, but unless we start imposing eugenics.

Age differences: The age of consent varies wildly, and with DOMA being struck down, why shouldn't a marriage to say, a 12 year old in one country or state, be valid and recognized in America?

It seems odd to "pick and choose" what moral exceptions apply to a marriage. Either it is a religious institution under those rules, or it's just a glorified contract that shouldn't really have any restrictions on it.

IF you want the government to recognize your union - Civil Union

Civil Unions between anybody/number of people.

Marriages - Whatever you can get a church or Pastor or some other holy man to perform the ceremony, go for it.

People married today with records held by the state and federal government should have those records tossed out. Anybody who still wants the benefits from the government should have to get a civil union in addition to their marriage certificate.
